title: The Right Focus in Leadership Leadership McCall, Casey
author: McCall, Casey
summary: McCall, a pastor, argues from both personal leadership experience and Paul's declaration to the Ephesian elders that good leadership must be process-focused because leaders can never guarantee outcomes. The argument is theological and practical: only God knows the full consequences of human decisions, and leaders who tie their self-evaluation to outcomes will either take unwarranted blame for bad results or unwarranted credit for good ones. The Tim Keller illustration grounds the point: Keller refused to write a parenting book despite raising three successful adult sons because he could not guarantee the outcome -- he recognized his own parenting failures and knew friends who were better parents had poorer outcomes. McCall's refinement: process-focus does not mean ignoring outcomes, it means orienting process toward viable goals while releasing control of results.
points: Good leadership must be process-focused because leaders can never guarantee outcomes -- the honest acknowledgment that outcome control exceeds human authority liberates leaders to evaluate themselves on what they can actually govern: the faithfulness and quality of the process.

Self-blame for bad outcomes and self-credit for good ones are symmetric errors: both assume the leader's process determines the result, when outcomes often reflect factors entirely outside the leader's control.

Paul's model from Acts 20:26 -- 'I am innocent of the blood of all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God' -- grounds leadership rest not in good results but in right process: he did what he was supposed to do.

Tim Keller's refusal to write a parenting book -- despite three successful adult sons -- is a model of wise leadership humility: taking credit for good outcomes their own process did not guarantee would be its own form of dishonesty.

Process-focus requires that goals orient the process: the preferable outcome informs the wise process, even though the wise process does not guarantee the preferable goal -- leaders must aim at something while releasing control of the landing.
quotes: Good leadership, therefore, must be process-focused leadership. Since the leader can never guarantee any outcome, wise leadership focuses on improving the process so that good outcomes are most likely.

Since we cannot always produce the exact outcomes we prefer, we should at least make sure we are pursuing truth, acting virtuously, following wise habits, and prioritizing faithfulness to God along the way. If our process is righteous, we can rest in the knowledge that the outcome resides in the loving hands of God.

Paul rests in the rightness of his process -- he declared the whole counsel of God. He did what he was supposed to do. Since he was faithful in the process, the outcome, whatever it turned out to be, would not be his responsibility.

Sometimes self-evaluation will reveal errors in our process. When that happens, we ought to respond with humility by admitting our role in the bad outcome and fixing what's broken in the process. Our new and improved process still won't guarantee good outcomes, but the experience of learning from our failures will make us better leaders going forward.

Keller responded that, even though their three boys had turned out well as adults, they didn't necessarily feel like they had been the best parents. In fact, they perceived that friends of theirs had been better parents than them without enjoying good outcomes.
Just as the wise leader can't always be blamed for bad outcomes, he never takes credit for good ones. God brings about good outcomes despite the leader's flaws.
